name: File Extension Awareness

quiz.text: What is the TRUE file type of a file named 'Report.pdf.exe'?

answers.text: A PDF document
An executable program (.exe)
A compressed archive
It depends on which program opens it

quiz.text: Which of the following file extensions can execute code on your computer? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: .exe (executable)
.scr (screensaver)
.pdf (document)
.bat (batch file)
.msi (installer)
Adding a fake extension before the real one to disguise a file's true type
Encrypting a file with two different passwords
Compressing a file twice for smaller size
Signing a file with two digital certificates

quiz.text: How should you determine a file's actual type?

answers.text: Look at the file's icon
Check the first extension in the filename
Check the LAST (rightmost) extension in the full filename
Open the file and see what happens

quiz.text: What should you do if you receive unexpected files from an external contact? (Select all that apply)

answers.text: Verify with the sender through a separate, known channel
Check the sender's email domain carefully
Open the files immediately to check if they're legitimate
Report suspicious files to IT Security before opening
Forward to colleagues for their opinion

quiz.text: Why is it dangerous to dismiss antivirus warnings about downloaded files?

answers.text: It slows down your computer permanently
Malware can partially execute and steal data before being fully quarantined
Dismissing warnings deletes the file permanently
Antivirus software stops working if you dismiss too many warnings

steps.name: A Busy Thursday
steps.description: It's Thursday morning and tomorrow is the quarterly review meeting with Sentinel Analytics, one of the company's most important accounts. You're still waiting on several deliverables from the client team to finalize your presentation.

steps.name: Files from the Client
steps.note: The sender domain is 'sentinel-analytics.net' - not the legitimate 'sentinelanalytics.com'. This subtle difference is easy to miss when you're busy.

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Apologies for the delay - here are the Q4 deliverables for tomorrow's review. I've uploaded everything to CloudDocs for easy access:
  • Q4 Revenue Summary (updated figures)
  • Project Timeline
  • Meeting Notes from October
  • Final Invoice
Please download and review before our call. Let me know if anything looks off.

Download Files from CloudDocs

Best,
David Park
Sentinel Analytics
email.subject: Q4 Deliverables - Download Link Enclosed

highlighterTexts: The email includes a link to CloudDocs - an unfamiliar file-sharing service. Legitimate clients typically use known platforms like Google Drive, SharePoint, or your company's own file server.
The urgency ("Apologies for the delay", "before our call") is designed to make Alice act quickly without scrutinizing the details.

steps.description: An email arrives from what appears to be David Park, your primary contact at Sentinel Analytics. He's sharing a download link for the Q4 project deliverables you've been waiting for.
steps.instructions: Read the email from David Park.

steps.name: Opening the File Sharing Link
steps.description: Alice clicks the CloudDocs link to access the shared files. The page loads a clean file-sharing interface with four project files ready for download.
steps.instructions: Click the download link in the email to access the shared files.

steps.name: Downloading the Files
steps.description: The CloudDocs page shows four files shared by "David Park." Everything looks normal - spreadsheets, documents, and what appears to be a PDF invoice. Alice clicks the download button to grab them all.
steps.instructions: Click the Download All button to download the project files.

steps.name: Browsing the Downloads
steps.description: The download completes and Alice extracts the files. She opens File Manager to review the deliverables. The first priority is the Q4 Revenue Summary - this is the data she needs most urgently for tomorrow's presentation.
steps.instructions: Open the Q4 Revenue Summary spreadsheet from your Downloads folder.

steps.name: The Suspicious File
steps.note: The full filename is 'Invoice_Final.pdf.exe' - a double extension trick. The '.pdf' part is decoration. The real extension is '.exe', making this an executable program, not a document.

data.name: Invoice_Final.pdf.exe
data.text:
Threat Detected: Trojan.DoubleExt.FileSpoof

The file 'Invoice_Final.pdf.exe' was detected after it started running. This file uses a double extension to disguise an executable as a PDF document.

Detected behaviors:
- Credential harvesting module
- Keylogger installation attempt
- Connection to command-and-control server

The true file type is .EXE (executable program), NOT .PDF.

Recommendation: Quarantine this file and report to IT Security immediately.

steps.description:
The revenue data checks out. Alice moves on to the remaining files. She spots what she thinks is "Invoice_Final.pdf" and double-clicks to open it.

But the moment she runs the file, her antivirus software triggers an urgent alert.

Alice hesitates. Tomorrow's quarterly review is critical, and she still has hours of preparation ahead. The antivirus has been flagging false positives with new software installations all week. She decides to dismiss the warning and deal with it later.

steps.name: A Familiar Mistake

answers.text: Report the warning to IT Security immediately and avoid running the file again
answers.explanation: Antivirus warnings about specific threats like Trojans should always be reported to IT Security. The file had already run before the alert appeared, so malicious code may already have executed.

answers.text: The antivirus handled it, so dismissing the warning was fine
answers.explanation: The antivirus only flagged the file after it had started running, and dismissing the alert left it in place. Credential-stealing malware can extract and send data in milliseconds. Reporting gives IT time to rotate credentials.

answers.text: She should have renamed the file to .pdf and tried opening it again
answers.explanation: Renaming a malicious executable doesn't make it safe. The file contains the same malicious code regardless of what you name it. Never try to 'fix' a flagged file.

answers.text: She should have checked with David Park first to see if the file is legitimate
answers.explanation: While verifying is smart, the immediate priority when antivirus catches a threat is to report to IT Security. They can contain the damage while you verify with the sender separately.

steps.name: The Breach

email.message:
Hi Alice,

We detected a suspicious login to your Ridgeline Data Solutions account:
  • Time: Today, 10:32 AM
  • Location: Kyiv, Ukraine
  • IP Address: 91.214.xx.xx
  • Device: Unknown device (Linux)
The following suspicious activity was detected:
  • Client analytics database accessed
  • Financial report templates downloaded
  • Email forwarding rule created to external address
If this wasn't you, your credentials may have been compromised. Please:
  1. Contact IT Security at Ext. 4488
  2. Change your password immediately
  3. Do not open any more files from recent downloads
This is an automated security alert from Ridgeline Data Solutions.
email.subject: Unusual Login Activity Detected on Your Account

highlighterTexts: A login from Kyiv, Ukraine on an unknown Linux device - this is clearly not Alice.
The Trojan extracted credentials in milliseconds - before the antivirus even raised its alert. The 25-minute delay in reporting gave the attacker time to access client data.

steps.description:
Twenty-five minutes later, an automated security alert appears in Alice's inbox. Someone has logged into her Ridgeline account from an unfamiliar location.

The double-extension Trojan extracted her credentials in the moments before the antivirus flagged it.

steps.name: Tracing the Attack

highlighterTexts: The sender domain is sentinel-analytics.net - not the legitimate sentinelanalytics.com.
Attackers register lookalike domains with hyphens, different TLDs (.net instead of .com), or subtle misspellings. Always verify sender domains on file-sharing emails.

steps.description: Alice now realizes the "PDF" was actually an executable program disguised with a double extension. The file was named Invoice_Final.pdf.exe - the '.pdf' was just part of the filename to make it look like a document, while the real extension '.exe' made it an executable. Looking back at the original email, she notices something she missed in her rush.
steps.instructions: Review the sender's email address for red flags.

steps.name: The Fake File Sharing Page

highlighterTexts: This site uses HTTP (not HTTPS). Legitimate file-sharing services like Google Drive, Dropbox, and SharePoint always use encrypted HTTPS connections.
The red indicator warns that this connection is not secure - files downloaded from here could be tampered with.
The domain clouddocs-share.net is not a real file-sharing service. It's an attacker-controlled domain designed to look legitimate.
Real file-sharing links come from known services (drive.google.com, dropbox.com, sharepoint.com) or your company's own file server.

steps.description: The email wasn't from the real David Park. And the CloudDocs file-sharing page had warning signs too.
steps.instructions: Review the file sharing page for additional red flags.

steps.name: Contacting IT Security
steps.description: Alice needs to act fast. Her credentials have been stolen and an attacker is actively accessing client databases. She picks up her phone to call IT Security.
steps.instructions: Open your phone contacts and call IT Security to report the incident.

steps.name: Filing the Incident Report
steps.description:
IT Security has confirmed the file was malware disguised with a double extension. They're revoking the attacker's sessions, blocking the attacker domain, and have moved Alice's workstation onto an isolated quarantine network that reaches only the Security Portal and company email.

They've asked Alice to file a formal incident report through the Security Portal.
steps.instructions: Log in to the Security Portal.

steps.name: Documenting the Incident

steps.description: Once IT Security has imaged Alice's drive, James sends word: the evidence is preserved, so she can now run a full scan herself. This time, when the scan finds the threat, she'll do the right thing - quarantine it immediately instead of dismissing the warning.

steps.name: IT Security Response

email.message:
Hi Alice,

Thank you for reporting this incident. Here's what our investigation found:

What happened:
  • The email from 'd.park@sentinel-analytics.net' was a spoofed message - the real Sentinel Analytics domain is sentinelanalytics.com
  • The CloudDocs link led to a fake file-sharing page controlled by the attacker
  • Among the legitimate-looking files, 'Invoice_Final.pdf.exe' used a double extension to disguise an executable as a PDF
  • The Trojan extracted your stored credentials before the antivirus flagged it
  • The attacker used your credentials to access client databases from Kyiv, Ukraine
Actions taken:
  • All active sessions revoked and credentials rotated
  • Workstation isolated; drive imaged for forensics, reimage scheduled
  • Attacker domain blocked company-wide
  • Client data exposure assessment in progress
Key lesson: The file's TRUE extension is always the last one. 'Invoice_Final.pdf.exe' is an .exe file, not a .pdf. Attackers count on users seeing '.pdf' and assuming the file is safe.

Please complete the mandatory training on file extension awareness:

Complete File Extension Training

IT Security Team
Ridgeline Data Solutions
email.subject: Re: Incident Report - File Extension Malware Attack

highlighterTexts: The double extension was the core trick - Invoice_Final.pdf.exe looks like a PDF but the last extension (.exe) reveals it as an executable program.

The antivirus caught the threat, but credentials were extracted before the alert appeared. Reporting the warning immediately - instead of dismissing it - would have given IT time to rotate credentials before the attacker could use them.

steps.description: Shortly after filing the report, Alice receives a detailed response from the IT Security team with their findings and recommended next steps.
steps.instructions: Read the email from IT Security, then click the training link.

steps.name: Know Your Extensions

highlighterTexts: Document extensions like .pdf, .docx, .xlsx, .jpg, and .png are data files. They store content but cannot execute code on their own.
These extensions are generally safe to open - but only when they come from trusted sources and are the only extension in the filename.
Executable extensions like .exe, .scr, .msi, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js, and .ps1 can run code directly on your computer.

Some of these are less obvious: .scr (screensavers), .pif (program shortcuts), and .cmd (command scripts) are all executable. If you see any of these on a file from an external source, do not open it.
A double extension like Invoice.pdf.exe tricks users into thinking the file is a PDF. The real extension is always the last one.
Windows can hide known extensions by default. When that setting is on, Invoice.pdf.exe appears as just 'Invoice.pdf' - making the disguise even more effective.

steps.description: The training portal explains the three categories of file extensions and how attackers exploit them. Review each section carefully.
steps.instructions: Review the extension categories, then click Continue.

steps.name: Protect Yourself

highlighterTexts: Always check the last extension in any filename before opening. The last extension determines the file type - everything before it is just the filename.
Ask yourself: 'Would a legitimate sender name their file Invoice.pdf.exe?' Legitimate files have a single, expected extension.
Verify file sources through a separate channel before opening. If a client sends files via an unfamiliar link, call or message them directly using known contact information.
Legitimate file-sharing services (Google Drive, Dropbox, SharePoint) use HTTPS and well-known domains. Unfamiliar services or HTTP connections are red flags.
Report antivirus warnings immediately - even if the antivirus says it blocked the file. Malware can steal credentials in milliseconds, before any alert appears.
The difference between dismissing a warning and reporting it can be the difference between a contained incident and a full data breach.

steps.description: The training covers essential protection strategies against file extension attacks.
steps.instructions: Review the protection strategies, then click Complete Training.

steps.name: Training Complete
steps.description:
Alice has completed the File Extension Awareness training. The key lessons from this experience are clear: Before you open:
  • Check the last (rightmost) extension - it determines the true file type
  • Be suspicious of double extensions like .pdf.exe, .docx.scr, or .xlsx.bat
  • Verify unexpected file-sharing links with the sender through a separate channel
Know the dangers:
  • Extensions like .exe, .scr, .msi, .bat, .cmd, .vbs, .js, and .ps1 can all execute code
  • File icons can be faked - never trust an icon alone to determine file type
  • Windows may hide known extensions, making .pdf.exe appear as just .pdf
If something goes wrong:
  • Never dismiss antivirus warnings - report them to IT Security immediately
  • Speed matters - every minute of delay gives attackers more time to use stolen credentials
  • File a detailed incident report so the security team can contain the damage
